name: Femi Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to employers, AI companies, unions or government, and your answers stay confidential. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Femi Ito, 27, and I lead a four-person carpentry crew on building sites. We set out walls and doors, check the measurements, then spend most of the day cutting, lifting and fitting things that never quite match the drawing. I like handing an apprentice a level and seeing him spot his own mistake; chasing missing timber and keeping everyone safe wears me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your position at work and home just now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've got a trade certificate, better pay than most hands on our sites, and enough savings for more than six months. I live with my partner Mara; we don't have children. There are plenty of other sites around, but I don't want to throw away a crew I've built because of a headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew to stop arguing with their phones and check the door frame with a square. A little help with orders is fine. A wall still has to stand straight when the inspector arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my pay stays where it is because clients still need someone who can make the drawings work on site. I'm saving already, though, because a late invoice can hurt even when plenty of builders are hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the same crew and put my usual amount into savings each payday. In the first year of this mild change, I'd try an AI ordering list on one small job only after our supplier shows it can count correctly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. The ordinary nuisance of missing materials bothers me more than a computer writing a list, and I can cover a slow month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why test the ordering list at all if you trust your own method?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring we ordered six doors for five openings because two versions of a drawing were in the folder. I'll let the tool compare the counts, but I'll still sign the purchase order myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mara if a project was delayed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Mara the delay is annoying, not a crisis. We'd leave the savings alone unless my wage actually stopped.

say: I would tell the crew to **check frames** with a square before trusting a screen.
I would accept small **ordering help** while keeping responsibility for the finished wall.
think: My **site pay** looks steady because clients still need skilled fitting.
I keep a **cash cushion** because late invoices can interrupt even good work.
do: Keep **leading the crew** on building sites at current hours.
Test an **AI ordering list** on one small job after the supplier demonstrates it.
feel: **Calm**, with ordinary irritation about late materials.
S0.quote: A wall still has to stand straight when the inspector arrives.
fieldNote: Femi treats **skilled fitting** as the source of his pay and uses physical inspection as his test of any software claim.
His strong savings absorb a delayed project, yet he remembers a real **ordering error** and is willing to trial a narrow tool.

steps.text: Keep leading the four-person carpentry crew on current sites
Test an AI ordering list on one small job after supplier demonstration

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office will be thinner before the saw benches are. If the software can plan deliveries, good, but a skipped delivery leaves my crew standing in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a cheaper planning team might let contractors bid lower and squeeze our rates next. I still expect steady paid site work for a while because robots are slower, and there are other sites nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our site manager to let me check the new schedules against what the crew can actually build. I'll learn that planning screen over a few evenings, then keep working full shifts during the first year and ask whether the crew rate changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy is fair. I don't expect my wages to vanish soon, but I dislike having a number on a screen decide how many hands we get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of planning would you check first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The delivery sequence. If plasterboard comes before the frame is ready, the hall fills up and we lose a morning moving it twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave if the rate fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what other contractors are paying before I made a speech. My partner Mara and I could take a short gap, but I'd still rather earn than live on savings.

say: I would warn that **site delays** still cost money even when software schedules deliveries.
I would welcome better planning if the crew can **check it**.
think: I expect **paid site work** to continue while robots spread slowly.
I worry cheaper office work could **squeeze rates** on our crew.
do: Learn the **planning screen** by checking schedules against real site work.
Keep **full shifts** and ask how the crew rate will change.
feel: **Uneasy** about staffing decisions coming from a screen.
S1.quote: I'd say the office will be thinner before the saw benches are.
fieldNote: He separates fast changes to **planning** from slower changes to physical carpentry, rather than treating all construction work alike.
His savings and nearby contractors give him room to question a **rate cut** without assuming he can safely stop earning.

steps.text: Learn the site planning screen over several evenings
Keep leading full carpentry shifts while checking the crew rate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger lads that a clever office machine isn't a carpenter yet, but we'd better watch the 2031 robot date. In 2028, someone still has to fix a twisted frame on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork and setting-out plans could move to AGI in two years; the lifting and fitting probably stay mine until the robots arrive about 2031. After that I expect fewer crew hours, even for someone good. My savings won't replace wages forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd ask the local technical college about a paid building inspection course and keep my site job while I study, if the timetable fits. In the first year after 2028, I'd use the AI plans only after checking measurements; I'd also apply for inspector trainee posts before 2031, when robots could take fitting work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about losing a large chunk of my wage in five years. I can make a plan, but it is a hard thing to tell an apprentice who just bought his first tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why inspection if the AI can think as well as you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't imagine an inspector's desk is safe from full AGI. I'm looking at the part where a person must visit a site and sign off, and I know robots could later do some of that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes at home now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Mara and I would put off replacing our car this winter. That keeps cash available for the course and for a gap between jobs if 2031 gets rough.

say: I would tell apprentices that **2028 AGI** changes plans before robots can fit timber.
I would warn the crew to watch the **2031 robot** arrival.
think: My **planning tasks** could move to AGI in 2028.
I expect **fewer paid hours** after hands-on robots arrive around 2031.
do: Ask about a **paid inspection course** while continuing site work.
Apply for **inspector trainee** posts before robots reach carpentry.
Postpone a **car replacement** to keep cash for training and a wage gap.
feel: **Anxious** about a major wage loss, though he can act.
S2.quote: My savings won't replace wages forever.
fieldNote: Femi identifies a **three-year bridge** between planning automation and physical robots, but does not mistake inspection for permanent safety.
His proposed **course** depends on pay and a workable timetable; delaying a car purchase protects cash while he keeps earning.

steps.text: Ask local technical college about paid building inspection course if timetable fits
Apply for inspector trainee posts before 2031
Postpone replacing the household car this winter
Keep leading carpentry shifts while studying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to teach good trades properly instead of pretending the machines are already here. The robot date is 2034, and nobody should sell a toolbox tomorrow because of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 32, when AGI arrives in 2031, I'd probably still be earning on site, though estimating and drawings would already be automated. At 35, if robots can do the fitting, I expect my crew's hours to fall; a good reputation may help me compete for fewer jobs, not save all four wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd talk to two small builders about whether they need a foreman who can coordinate repairs, and I'd keep my present crew together. By 2032 I'd complete a site safety qualification if the evening course stays affordable; in the first year after 2031 I'd use AI estimates and keep checking them against timber used on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, though the extra years let me breathe. I could build another skill while wages still come in, which is different from borrowing to study in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run your own contracting business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe later, after I've seen the builders' books. I won't put my savings into a van just because a ten-year prediction sounds tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do the apprentices fit that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn repairs as well as new builds, since old houses don't read plans. I can't promise them 2034 jobs, and pretending I can would be unfair.

say: I would tell the crew the **2034 robot** date gives us years to prepare.
I would urge apprentices to learn **repairs** as well as new builds.
think: My **site wages** likely continue when AGI changes estimates in 2031.
My crew could lose **paid hours** when fitting robots arrive around 2034.
do: Ask two builders about **repair foreman** work while leading my crew.
Complete an affordable **site safety qualification** by 2032 if available.
Check **AI estimates** against actual timber after 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to prepare without emergency borrowing.
S3.quote: At 35, if robots can do the fitting, I expect my crew's hours to fall; a good reputation may help me compete for fewer jobs, not save all four wages.
fieldNote: He sees **2031 AGI** affecting estimating while hands-on work lasts nearer 2034, when his crew faces an income shock.
His interest in **repair coordination** grows from present site experience, and he resists buying a van before testing demand.

steps.text: Ask two small builders about repair foreman vacancies this year
Complete affordable evening site safety qualification by 2032 if available
Check AI estimates against timber used on site after 2031
Keep leading the current four-person carpentry crew

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time to get an honest return from a trade certificate and pass it on. I'll be 37 when AGI arrives in 2036 and 40 when the robots arrive around 2039, not anywhere near retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My present carpentry skill could still earn through much of the decade, but I expect the physical jobs to narrow by 2039. Ten years helps me change course, yet it doesn’t turn my savings into a lifetime income or make family plans simple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the better-paying site jobs now and add to savings from each contract. Over the next two years I'd try one paid repair-coordination job on weekends before investing in a business; in 2037 I'd use AGI for schedules while keeping site shifts, then review whether enough repair work remains before robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy now because the wage threat is distant enough to work on. I'd feel worse if I spent ten years saying a skilled pair of hands can never be copied.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about children in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Mara and I haven't made that decision. I wouldn't tell her we must wait for 2039, but I'd want a real income plan before taking on a bigger home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you the repair path is viable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three paying customers over a few months, not just compliments from friends. I'd write down what each job earned after materials and travel before buying a van.

say: I would say a **decade** gives me time to earn and teach my trade.
I would remind apprentices that I will be **40**, still needing wages, when robots arrive.
think: My **carpentry income** could narrow when robots arrive around 2039.
My savings cannot fund **early retirement** or settle family plans alone.
do: Keep taking **paid site jobs** and add earnings to savings.
Try a **paid repair job** before spending on a business.
Use **AGI schedules** in 2037 while checking demand for repairs.
feel: **Uneasy** about later wages, with time to test another path.
S4.quote: Ten years helps me change course, yet it doesn’t turn my savings into a lifetime income or make family plans simple.
fieldNote: The decade lowers his near-term pressure, yet he correctly places himself at **working age** when physical robots reach sites.
He wants evidence from **paying repair customers** before committing savings to a van or assuming a future business will support a family.

steps.text: Keep accepting better-paying carpentry shifts on current sites
Add part of each contract payment to savings
Try one paid weekend repair-coordination job within two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because the robots arrive in 2031 before I've built another way to earn. A paid course with evening hours and clear trainee vacancies would help more than a speech about being adaptable. I'd still need the site wage while learning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens to the apprentices when the crew shrinks. If I lose a day's work, I have savings; a first-year apprentice may miss rent. I'd want contractors to show them real openings, not just offer another unpaid certificate.

headlineQuote: If I lose a day's work, I have savings; a first-year apprentice may miss rent.
portrait: Femi is a **27-year-old** carpentry lead with strong savings, higher pay and many nearby sites.
He trusts **measured work** and tries technology after someone demonstrates it.
He expects **AGI planning** to change before robots threaten physical fitting and crew hours.
His plans keep **paid work** alongside training, with concern for apprentices who have less savings.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** leaves too little time to build another income before 2031 robots shrink crew work.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid evening course** with clear inspector trainee vacancies would let him retrain while keeping site wages.
